4628               	; 		' itself out: "it animates a little bit and goes out". Nothing fails,
4629               	; 		' because both writes are perfectly valid and land exactly where they
4630               	; 		' were addressed -- they just carry the same sixteen bytes.

4632               	; 		' The lit call staged at nesb(0); this one stages sixteen bytes up.
4633               	; 		' nesb is 96 bytes for the escalator's six characters and the
4634               	; 		' escalator never runs on the title screen, so the room is free. The
4635               	; 		' pointer is put back immediately: esc_tick stages at offset 0 and
4636               	; 		' would otherwise write its six characters one tile off.

4766               	;
4767               	; 	' 8-3-8 IS EDGE-TRIGGERED AND ANY STRAY DIGIT RESETS IT (see title_wait).
4768               	; 	'
4769               	; 	' It used to read cont1.key raw every pass and test only for the digit it
4770               	; 	' wanted next. That worked -- but only because 8-3-8 ALTERNATES, so holding
4771               	; 	' 8 cannot advance past the first step. It is an accident of the sequence
4772               	; 	' rather than a design, and it had two costs: 8,5,3,9,8 opened this page as
4773               	; 	' readily as 8,3,8, and a key that READS as held for many frames got a free
4774               	; 	' walk through the state machine.
4775               	; 	'
4776               	; 	' That second one is not hypothetical on this machine. ALPHA LOCK shorts a
4777               	; 	' keyboard line -- and Classic99 defaults to invertcaps, so it reads DOWN
4778               	; 	' with the host's Caps Lock UP -- and this page was reached twice from
4779               	; 	' single keypresses while testing an unrelated change.
4780               	; 	'
4781               	; 	' The reset is the DEFAULT rather than a test for a particular wrong digit:
4782               	; 	' Bust-A-Bobble resets only on a stray 3 and still lets 8,5,3,8 through.
4783               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------------- 838 setup page

5508               	;
5509               	; 	' ======================================================================
5510               	; 	' DRAWING THE STORE -- four blits, once per screen crossing
5511               	; 	' ======================================================================
5512               	; 	' This is the whole cost of the flip, and it is paid on a discrete event
5513               	; 	' rather than every frame. RallyX's pan repaints 576 chars every time the
5514               	; 	' camera moves one cell; this repaints 640 about once every two seconds
5515               	; 	' of running.
5516               	; 	' SPRITES OFF BEFORE THE BLIT, NOT AFTER IT. This routine WAITs between
5517               	; 	' bands -- one band a frame, because a burst of VDP writes past a few
5518               	; 	' dozen in one frame is silently dropped -- so painting the new screen
5519               	; 	' takes several frames, and for all of them the OLD screen's actors and
5520               	; 	' obstacles were still sitting on top of it. Following Harry through a
5521               	; 	' seam showed him and every cart from the floor he had just left,
5522               	; 	' standing on a shop that was assembling itself underneath them.
5523               	; 	'
5524               	; 	' They are put back by the normal draw on the same pass, so the crossing
5525               	; 	' reads as a cut rather than as a dissolve with ghosts in it.
5526               	; 	' EACH BAND IS FINISHED BEFORE THE FRAME IT IS DRAWN IN ENDS, and the
5527               	; 	' bands go TOP DOWN. Both halves of that matter.
5528               	; 	'
5529               	; 	' The blit paints the template -- shelves, pillars and all -- and the
5530               	; 	' radios and prizes then take out the fixtures they stand in. Those two
5531               	; 	' used to be four frames apart: all four bands blitted with a WAIT
5532               	; 	' between them, and only afterwards the clearing. So every screen change
5533               	; 	' showed its counters and beams for several frames and then erased them,
5534               	; 	' which reads as the shop flickering rather than as it being drawn.
5535               	; 	'
5536               	; 	' TOP DOWN because a band's beam tops are stamped into the SLAB ROW OF
5537               	; 	' THE BAND ABOVE. Going bottom-up, band 1's blit would paint over the
5538               	; 	' beam tops band 0 had just put there. Going top-down the band above is
5539               	; 	' always already drawn, so everything a band needs -- its own cells and
5540               	; 	' the row it borrows overhead -- is final by the time its WAIT arrives.
5541               	; 	'
5542               	; 	' `3 - dq` rather than `FOR dlv = 3 TO 0 STEP -1`: dlv is an unsigned
5543               	; 	' byte, so counting down past zero wraps to 255 and the loop never ends
5544               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A).
5545               	; draw_screen:
5546               cvb_DRAW_SCREEN
5547               	; 	#if NES
5548               	; 	' AND BLACK BACK FOR THE STORE -- see the note in title_draw. Index 0 is
5549               	; 	' the universal backdrop, so the dark blue the title sets would otherwise

5551               	; 	'
5552               	; 	' A DARK BLUE BACKDROP WAS TRIED HERE, to give the sunset a fourth band
5553               	; 	' (see nes_inkmap in assets/nes_chr.asm). It works, and it costs the

5618               	; 		#ddst = #ddst + 96		' three rows down -- see the overscan note
5619               	; 		' ONE ROW A FRAME, AND THIS IS WHY THREE BANDS IN FOUR LOST THEIR
5620               	; 		' LAST TWO ROWS. The NMI copies PPUBUF into the PPU during vblank
5621               	; 		' and its copy loop DOES NOT STOP WHEN VBLANK ENDS -- it runs to
5622               	; 		' the end of the descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and a
5623               	; 		' PPUDATA write outside vblank is discarded by the hardware.
5624               	; 		'
5625               	; 		' NTSC gives about 2273 CPU cycles of vblank, OAM DMA takes 513 of
5626               	; 		' them, and the copy costs roughly 14 a byte: about a hundred bytes
5627               	; 		' get through. A 32x5 band is 160, so the last sixty-odd vanished
5628               	; 		' -- three whole rows arrived, the fourth stopped eight or nine
5629               	; 		' cells in, and the floor bar and the air row above it were simply
5630               	; 		' never there. Measured on screen as `#########.......`, on every
5631               	; 		' band whose blit did not happen to start early.
5632               	; 		'
5633               	; 		' A row is 32 bytes, which fits with room to spare. This costs four
5634               	; 		' extra frames per band at round start and nothing during play.

5693               	; 	' A SUPPORT BEAM HAS TO REACH THE FLOOR IT HOLDS UP, AND THAT FLOOR IS
5694               	; 	' NOT IN ITS OWN BAND. A beam fills its band's four air rows, so its top

5696               	; 	' five pixels of bar over three of green (see SLAB), so the beam stopped

5698               	; 	' misses the floor, which is exactly what it was.

5703               	; 	' band blits go down first and the tops are stamped afterwards, from a

6334               	; 			' PER KIND, not one global speed (see start_krook).
6335               	; 			' THE SPEED IS A PROPERTY OF THE KIND, and obs() only ever
6336               	; 			' held a copy of it -- set from the kind here, zeroed for a
6337               	; 			' radio below, and read in one place. upd_obst derives it
6338               	; 			' from obk() instead, which is 8 bytes of RAM back and one
6339               	; 			' fewer thing that can disagree with itself.
6340               	; 			' THEY COME FROM THE FAR SIDE. Kelly walked into this screen
6341               	; 			' from one edge, so the obstacles start at the OTHER edge and
6342               	; 			' run toward him. Crossing a seam then always presents an
6343               	; 			' ONCOMING stream, never a set of backs he has to catch up
6344               	; 			' with -- and it means the direction he is travelling is
6345               	; 			' always the direction the danger comes from.

6348               	; 			' an absolute position, and the slot index spreads them out

6352               	; 			' THAT DISTANCE IS SET BY THE JUMP.
6353               	; 			'
6354               	; 			' It used to be `(lx AND 63) + 64` -- a masked byte out of
6355               	; 			' the placement table plus a constant -- so the gap between
6356               	; 			' the two hazards was whatever those two bytes happened to
6357               	; 			' differ by. Measured across the five populated screens it

6361               	; 			' reported from play.

6364               	; 			' closes on an oncoming hazard at (KWALK64 + its speed)/64

6366               	; 			' eats 82 px of closing distance at the fastest hazard. At

6484               	; 			' THE BALL IS ON THE GROUND WHEN HE GETS TO IT.
6485               	; 			'
6486               	; 			' The bounce phase used to be `lx AND 31` -- a byte out of
6487               	; 			' the placement table, which is to say arbitrary. Run onto
6488               	; 			' a screen and the first ball might be at the bottom of its
6489               	; 			' arc, where a jump clears it, or at the top, where it has
6490               	; 			' to be ducked, and nothing on the way in told you which.
6491               	; 			' Sometimes you could keep running and jump it; sometimes
6492               	; 			' the same approach at the same speed could not be jumped
6493               	; 			' at all. That is not difficulty, it is a coin toss.
6494               	; 			'
6495               	; 			' So the phase is worked BACKWARDS from the meeting. He
6496               	; 			' closes 4 px a pass and the ball 2, so they meet in
6497               	; 			' (gap / 6) passes; the phase advances one a pass and wraps
6498               	; 			' at 32, so seeding it with the NEGATIVE of that lands it on
6499               	; 			' phase 0 -- the ground -- exactly as they arrive.
6500               	; 			'
6501               	; 			' The gap is the same either way round: he enters at one
6502               	; 			' wall and the ball starts `stag` in from the other, so it
6503               	; 			' is 232 - stag whichever direction the floor runs.
6504               	; 			'
6505               	; 			' It stays forgiving rather than exact. The arc is flat near
6506               	; 			' the bottom, so anything within eight passes either side is
6507               	; 			' still under the jump; and it only holds for an unbroken
6508               	; 			' run, which is the case the player is entitled to read off
6509               	; 			' the screen. Duck, stop or take a hit and everything after
6510               	; 			' is out of step again -- which is the game.
6511               	; 			' obp is a BALL-only field: upd_obst reads it under an
6512               	; 			' IF uk = OB_BALL and nothing else touches it, and every
6513               	; 			' ball has it computed below. It was seeded here from a
6514               	; 			' table byte that no longer exists, and for anything but
6515               	; 			' a ball that seed was never read.
6516               	; 			IF lk = OB_BALL THEN

8981               	;
8982               	; 	' THE VICTROLA, AS CHARACTERS. It never moves, so a sprite spent a
8983               	; 	' scan-line slot on something that can be painted once when the screen is
8984               	; 	' drawn -- and at one 16x16 sprite it could only ever be one colour and
8985               	; 	' one size. Four cells is twice the area for no sprite at all.
8986               	; 	'
8987               	; 	' It stands ON the slab, so it fills the band's rows 2 and 3; row 4 is
8988               	; 	' the floor bar itself -- and a PRIZE uses those same two rows.
8989               	; 	'
8990               	; 	' THEY CAN SHARE A BAND, AND THE CLAIM THAT USED TO BE HERE WAS WRONG.
8991               	; 	' It said the two never share a screen because "genstore keeps prizes off
8992               	; 	' the screens that carry hazards". That stopped being true the moment
8993               	; 	' hazard placement moved into the per-Krook stor_lvl table, and nothing
8994               	; 	' noticed, because the prize table is not part of the level table and
8995               	; 	' every check was written about one object at a time. Two money bags ended
8996               	; 	' up standing on a radio -- not fighting it, since the two routines poke
8997               	; 	' different cells and the later writer simply wins, so they read as one
8998               	; 	' merged object.
8999               	; 	'
9000               	; 	' WHAT KEEPS THEM APART IS COLUMNS. A radio stands at column 7, 15 or 23
9001               	; 	' (see lrc below); genstore's _off_the_rack nudges a prize clear of all
9002               	; 	' three, and checklevels.py reads that arithmetic back out of THIS file
9003               	; 	' and fails the build on any overlap.
9004               	; 	'
9005               	; 	' rdall = 1 paints all four cells, 0 repaints only the top-right one --
9006               	; 	' the pulse. Same address arithmetic either way, so the two cannot drift.
9007               	; 	' A BEAM TOP HANGS OUT OF THE FLOOR ABOVE, and the beam it belongs to has
9008               	; 	' just been taken away. `beam_tops` stamps SLABP -- the floor bar with the
9009               	; 	' support carried up through its lower three pixel rows -- into the slab
9010               	; 	' row above every pillar, and it runs BEFORE the radios and prizes are
9011               	; 	' placed. Clearing a pillar's own cells therefore left three grey pixels
9012               	; 	' dangling from the ceiling with nothing under them.
9013               	; 	'
9014               	; 	' TESTED, NOT ASSUMED: only SLABP is put back to SLAB. The row above the
9015               	; 	' top shopping floor is the ROOF DECK, a different character altogether,
9016               	; 	' and writing a floor bar over it would punch a hole in the roof.
9017               	; 	' A SHELF RUN IS FIVE CELLS WIDE and a radio covers two, so one standing
9018               	; 	' on a counter punched a hole through its middle and left the ends either
9019               	; 	' side -- the same incoherence the dangling pillar had, and worse, because
9020               	; 	' a counter reads as one object. The whole unit goes: walk outward along
9021               	; 	' the band's row 2 while the cell is still a shelf top, clearing it and
9022               	; 	' its bottom half together.
9023               	; 	'
9024               	; 	' Bounded at eight steps. The runs are five, so eight is slack rather
9025               	; 	' than a guess -- and an unbounded walk would run off the end of the row
9026               	; 	' if the name table ever held something unexpected.
9027               	; 	#if NES
9028               	; 	' WHAT THE TEMPLATE PUT IN THIS CELL, for a target that cannot read its
9029               	; 	' own video memory back. #nta is the offset INSIDE the band (0-159) and
9030               	; 	' nbl is the band; the answer is the byte SCREEN blitted there.
9031               	; 	'
9032               	; 	' This is the same arithmetic the blit itself does in draw_band --
9033               	; 	' template id out of stor_ix for (band, screen), times 160, plus the
9034               	; 	' offset -- so the two cannot disagree about what is on screen. It is
9035               	; 	' reading what the cell MEANS, not guessing from where the cell is: a
9036               	; 	' coordinate is a fact about this layout, the character is a fact about
9037               	; 	' the world, and only the second is safe to erase on.
9038               	; 	' SIXTEEN PATTERNS INTO THE BORROWED SLOTS, ONE VBLANK EACH.
9039               	; 	'
9040               	; 	' This is what esc_stand and esc_run cost on this machine. Four sprites is
9041               	; 	' 16 patterns and **a tile here is SIXTEEN bytes** -- two bitplanes -- so
9042               	; 	' the swap is 256 bytes. Three ways to spend that, and only one works:
9043               	; 	'
9044               	; 	'   nes_def         rendering off, ~2 frames of DARK SCREEN every mount.
9045               	; 	'                   This is the flash that was reported for three sessions.
9046               	; 	'   resident art    no upload at all -- but it needs 16 free patterns per
9047               	; 	'                   facing and there are only twelve free in the whole
9048               	; 	'                   table. Tried, and it overwrote Harry's left-facing legs.
9049               	; 	'   queued, chunked <- this. 64 bytes a vblank, four vblanks, picture up
9050               	; 	'                   the whole time.
9051               	; 	'
9052               	; 	' FOUR CHUNKS BECAUSE ONE WILL NOT FIT. The NMI's copy loop runs to the end
9053               	; 	' of its descriptor whatever the raster is doing, and the PPUADDR/PPUSCROLL
9054               	; 	' restore that follows it re-points the PPU mid-frame if it runs late --
9055               	; 	' which is the whole picture jumping for a frame. About 1679 cycles are
9056               	; 	' available after OAM DMA and a copy costs 50 + 14 a byte, so 64 bytes
9057               	; 	' (946) is comfortable and 256 (3634) is not. The WAITs are load-bearing:
9058               	; 	' PPUBUF accumulates for a whole pass, so without them all four descriptors
9059               	; 	' would flush in one vblank and cost exactly what the single call did.
9060               	; 	' checkvblank.py sums the descriptors BETWEEN WAITs for this reason.
9061               	; 	'
9062               	; 	' The cost is four frames at a mount or a dismount, once each, against two
9063               	; 	' frames of black. The caller sets #nsrc; nes_chrinit copies nchr, ncnt,
9064               	; 	' #ncol and nink into zero page rather than consuming the variables, so
9065               	; 	' they only need setting once.
9066               	; 	'
9067               	; 	' THE INTERMEDIATE STATE IS VISIBLE and that is accepted: for a frame or
9068               	; 	' two Harry is part standing and part running. He is stepping onto a
9069               	; 	' staircase at the time, which is exactly when a limb changing shape reads
9070               	; 	' as him changing pose.
9071               	; nes_swp16:
9072               	; 	' HARRY COMES OFF THE SCREEN FIRST, because this takes four frames.
9073               	; 	'
9074               	; 	' The swap is 256 bytes and a vblank carries about a hundred, so it goes as
9075               	; 	' four queued chunks with a WAIT between them (see below). The game loop is
9076               	; 	' stopped for those frames but the PPU is not, so whatever is half-written
9077               	; 	' is on screen: for a frame or two Harry was part standing and part
9078               	; 	' running -- reported as a glitch when he steps off a flight, and it is
9079               	; 	' one. All four of his sprites differ between the two poses, so there is no
9080               	; 	' ordering of the chunks that stays coherent.
9081               	; 	'
9082               	; 	' He is hidden instead. Four frames of absence at the exact moment he steps
9083               	; 	' on or off a staircase reads as nothing at all, where a figure assembled
9084               	; 	' out of two poses reads as a fault. draw_actors puts him back on its next
9085               	; 	' pass -- no flag to clear, because it writes all four slots every time.
9086               	; 	'
9087               	; 	' AND THE OAM MIRRORS WITH HIM. nes_oam2 copies slots 0-27 into 28-55 to
9088               	; 	' make each 16x16 actor two NES sprites, and it only runs at the end of
9089               	; 	' draw_actors -- which is not running during these WAITs. Without the call
9090               	; 	' below his left half would vanish and his RIGHT half would stay, which is
9091               	; 	' a worse artefact than the one being fixed.
9092               	; 	SPRITE 4,SPRHID,0,0,0
9093               	; 	SPRITE 5,SPRHID,0,0,0
9094               	; 	SPRITE 6,SPRHID,0,0,0
9095               	; 	SPRITE 7,SPRHID,0,0,0
9096               	; 	ASM JSR nes_oam2
9097               	; 	nchr = P_HSTB
9098               	; 	ntab = 0
9099               	; 	#ncol = 0
9100               	; 	nink = 1
9101               	; 	ncnt = 4
9102               	; 	WAIT
9103               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9104               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32		' four patterns of source art, 8 bytes each
9105               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9106               	; 	WAIT
9107               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9108               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
9109               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9110               	; 	WAIT
9111               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9112               	; 	#nsrc = #nsrc + 32
9113               	; 	nchr = nchr + 4
9114               	; 	WAIT
9115               	; 	GOSUB nes_escd
9116               	; 	RETURN
9117               	;
9118               	; nes_def:
9119               	; 	' WHAT DEFINE WOULD HAVE DONE. CVBasic implements no DEFINE at all for the
9120               	; 	' NES, on the reading that patterns live in cartridge CHR ROM -- but an
9121               	; 	' iNES header with a CHR-bank count of ZERO asks for 8 KB of CHR-RAM
9122               	; 	' instead, and that is the header CVBasic emits whenever the program uses
9123               	; 	' no BITMAP/CHRROM statement. So the pattern table here is ordinary VRAM
9124               	; 	' and this is the write. assets/nes_chr.asm carries the routine and the
9125               	; 	' reasoning; the caller sets #nsrc, nchr, ncnt and ntab.
9126               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrup
9127               	; 	RETURN
9128               	;
9129               	; 	' AND THE SAME THING WITHOUT LOSING A FRAME. nes_def turns rendering off
9130               	; 	' and waits for a vblank the NMI therefore never services, so the game's
9131               	; 	' own WAIT then waits for the one after -- about two frames a call. That
9132               	; 	' is free at setup and ruinous anywhere that runs repeatedly. It builds
9133               	; 	' the same bytes into `nesb` and hands the NMI a single copy descriptor
9134               	; 	' instead. See assets/nes_chr.asm.
9135               	; 	'
9136               	; 	' THE NAME IS HISTORICAL: it was written for esc_tick, which redefines six
9137               	; 	' characters EVERY PASS on the two escalator screens and ran visibly slow
9138               	; 	' on nes_def. Nothing about it is escalator-specific -- it takes the same
9139               	; 	' inputs as nes_def plus #nesb, and the title's marquee uses it too, where
9140               	; 	' nes_def was switching the picture off twice a step and reading as a
9141               	; 	' flashing title screen.
9142               	; 	'
9143               	; 	' #nesb must point at a buffer of at least ncnt*16 bytes and is set once
9144               	; 	' in init_tables, which runs before boot: and therefore before the title.
9145               	; nes_escd:
9146               	; 	ASM JSR nes_chrq
9147               	; 	RETURN
9148               	;
9149               	; nes_tpl:
9150               	; 	nti = lv8(nbl)
9151               	; 	nti = nti + klsc
9152               	; 	#ntb = #stix + nti
9153               	; 	ntd = PEEK(#ntb)
9154               	; 	#ntc = #tsrc(ntd)
9155               	; 	#ntc = #ntc + #nta
9156               	; 	#ntc = #ntc + #sttp
9157               	; 	ntv = PEEK(#ntc)
9158               	; 	RETURN

9242               	; 	' A PILLAR'S CAP MAY BE CLEARED; AN END WALL'S MAY NOT. beam_one stamps
9243               	; 	' both into the slab row of the band above, but they mean different
9244               	; 	' things. SLABP is the top of a free-standing pillar: a radio or a prize
9245               	; 	' stands in front of the pillar, so leaving its cap up there hangs a grey
9246               	; 	' stub over the fixture and that is what this routine exists to remove.
9247               	; 	' SLABE and ROOFSE are written ONLY at column 0 and column 31 -- read
9248               	; 	' beam_one, they are the two edge cases -- and there they are the
9249               	; 	' BUILDING'S OUTSIDE WALL, carrying its brick bond up through the floor
9250               	; 	' above. Clearing those took the support out from under the storey above
9251               	; 	' at the very edge of the screen, so the second floor visibly rested on
9252               	; 	' nothing.
9253               	; 	'
9254               	; 	' It could only ever show on the ESCALATOR screens, which is exactly how
9255               	; 	' it was reported -- one side, then mirrored on the other. The flight
9256               	; 	' fills the middle of an escalator band, so that screen's radio or prize
9257               	; 	' is pushed right out against the end wall; on every other screen no
9258               	; 	' fixture sits close enough for the two-cell clear at #bca and #bca+1 to
9259               	; 	' reach column 0 or 31.

9261               cvb_BEAM_CLEAR
9262               	; 	' A BEAM TOP IS NOT IN THE TEMPLATE. beam_one VPOKEs it into the row
9263               	; 	' ABOVE each band, out of the pillar-column table -- so on the NES this
9264               	; 	' asks that same table rather than the PPU, and #bca sits one row above
9265               	; 	' the band, which is why it cannot go through nes_tpl.
9266               	; 	'
9267               	; 	' IT ALSO REPRODUCES beam_one'S EXCLUSION OF COLUMNS 0 AND 31. Those
9268               	; 	' carry SLABE/ROOFSE, the building's OUTSIDE WALL, not a pillar cap --

9889               	; 	' ======================================================================
9890               	; 	' OBSTACLES
9891               	; 	' ======================================================================
9892               	; upd_obst:
9893               cvb_UPD_OBST
9894               	; 	' ONE ACCUMULATOR PER KIND, NOT PER SLOT. Every hazard of a kind moves at
9895               	; 	' that kind's speed, so three calls a pass serve all eight slots.
9896               	; 	'
9897               	; 	' Per-slot would have meant up to eight calls of O(fdv) work every pass --
9898               	; 	' the positive feedback loop CLAUDE.md 3A warns about, where a slow pass is
9899               	; 	' made slower by the very code meant to take the loop rate out of the
9900               	; 	' game's behaviour. It also saves the eight bytes an obacc() would cost,
9901               	; 	' and ColecoVision RAM is the tighter budget.
9902               	; 	pacc = oacb

10192               	;
10193               	; 	' ONE STEP OF A FRACTIONAL SPEED, FOR WHOEVER IS MOVING.
10194               	; 	'
10195               	; 	' `pacc` in and out, `psp64` in (sixty-fourths of a pixel per FRAME),
10196               	; 	' `pspd` out (whole pixels this pass). CVBasic has no locals, so the caller
10197               	; 	' stages its own accumulator in and takes it back out; that costs four
10198               	; 	' statements against the fourteen this used to be, written out per actor.
10199               	; 	'
10200               	; 	' Harry had the only copy. Kelly, the hazards and the bounce phase all need
10201               	; 	' the same thing -- everything the round clock judges has to advance by
10202               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAMES, or the loop rate becomes a difficulty dial and where the
10203               	; 	' player stands decides the outcome (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10204               	; 	'
10205               	; 	' TWO DRAINS CAP THE STEP AT 2 PER FRAME whatever psp64 says (CLAUDE.md
10206               	; 	' 3A: N drains cap the speed at N, and the surplus leaks into a byte that
10207               	; 	' wraps). Every caller is under that: Kelly 102/64 = 1.6, the fastest
10208               	; 	' hazard 76/64 = 1.2, Harry 57/64 = 0.9, the bounce phase 25/64 = 0.4.
10209               	; 	'
10210               	; 	' FIVE FRAMES, AND THREE WAS TOO FEW. At 2 px a frame five frames is 10 px,
10211               	; 	' and to skip a position window an actor must start outside it on one side
10212               	; 	' and land outside on the other, which needs 12. Three was the original bug
10213               	; 	' in miniature: the lift screen runs at almost exactly 20 passes a second,
10214               	; 	' which IS fdv = 3, so every hitch there lost a frame. The clamp exists for
10215               	; 	' a genuine stall and at five it only fires for one.

10704               	; 	' THE SIXTEENTH-PIXEL ACCUMULATOR. hx is one unsigned byte per screen
10705               	; 	' (2), so there is nowhere to keep a fraction -- the fraction lives here
10706               	; 	' and is spent as whole pixels. THREE IFs, not a loop and not a divide:
10707               	; 	' `%` and `/` both compile to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and this
10708               	; 	' runs every pass.
10709               	; 	'
10710               	; 	' THE NUMBER OF DRAINS IS A CEILING ON THE SPEED, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE
10711               	; 	' POINT OF THIS COMMENT. Each IF can spend one whole pixel, so N drains
10712               	; 	' cap hspd at N px per pass NO MATTER WHAT hsp64 SAYS. The invariant is:
10713               	; 	'
10714               	; 	'     hacc is under 16 on entry, and hsp64 is at most 48,
10715               	; 	'     so hacc is under 64 here and three drains always suffice.
10716               	; 	'
10717               	; 	' KEEP hsp64 <= 48. This was quarter-pixels with TWO drains and the same
10718               	; 	' invariant written the same way -- "hsp4 is at most 8, so it can never
10719               	; 	' need a third" -- and it was correct until somebody set hsp4 = 9 without
10720               	; 	' re-reading it. The crook then ran at a flat 2.0 px/pass while every
10721               	; 	' comment, the design table and assets/checkchase.py all said 2.25, and
10722               	; 	' the surplus quarter leaked into hacc and wrapped the byte every 256
10723               	; 	' passes. Nothing failed; he simply arrived two thirds of a screen short
10724               	; 	' of his own escape. checkchase.py now counts these IFs and refuses a
10725               	; 	' speed the drains cannot deliver.
10726               	; 	'
10727               	; 	' 7, NOT 6, AND THE REASON IS MEASURED. Tracked off the reference video
10728               	; 	' (DESIGN.md 4a), the 2600's Kelly covers 0.40 screen widths a second and
10729               	; 	' its Harry 0.193 -- a ratio of 2.07. At hsp4 = 6 ours was 2.67, and the
10730               	; 	' crook visibly strolled. 7 brings it to 2.29. 8 would match the original
10731               	; 	' exactly and cannot be used: Kelly's route here is 1.95x Harry's, so a
10732               	; 	' speed ratio of 2.0 leaves the on-foot chase 0.2 s of slack, which is no
10733               	; 	' chase at all. checkchase.py holds the line.
10734               	; 	' STILL RUNNING FROM THE STAIRS -- and this has to come BEFORE the move,
10735               	; 	' not after it. It sat below the two `IF hmv` blocks, where all it could
10736               	; 	' still reach was the animation counter: he faced the right way, played
10737               	; 	' the run cycle and did not travel a pixel. He stood at the foot of the
10738               	; 	' flight looking busy.
10739               	; 	'
10740               	; 	' TWO THINGS END THE RUN, AND BOTH ARE VISIBLE ON SCREEN.
10741               	; 	'

10835               	; 	' HE WALKS BY REAL TIME, NOT BY LOOP PASS -- one accumulate-and-drain per
10836               	; 	' ELAPSED FRAME rather than per pass. Everything that moves here used to be
10837               	; 	' per pass while the CLOCK is paced by the frame delta, so a busy screen
10838               	; 	' slowed Harry in real seconds and the clock did not slow with him: the
10839               	; 	' same uninterrupted escape finished with nine timer units in hand from a
10840               	; 	' light screen and none at all from the lift screen, decided by where the
10841               	; 	' player happened to be standing. Now he covers the same ground per second
10842               	; 	' wherever anybody is (DESIGN.md 0f-ter).
10843               	; 	'
10844               	; 	' A LOOP, NOT A MULTIPLY. `*` compiles to a real TMS9900 MPY, and reading a
10845               	; 	' 16-bit variable straight after one returns the product's HIGH word
10846               	; 	' (CLAUDE.md 3A). fdv is 1..3 here, so this is at most three adds.
10847               	; 	'
10848               	; 	' SIXTY-FOURTHS, AND ONLY TWO DRAINS -- both fall out of accumulating per
10849               	; 	' FRAME instead of per pass. He covers under a pixel a frame, so two drains
10850               	; 	' are ample where the per-pass version needed three; and the finer unit is
10851               	; 	' what makes the speed tunable at all. In sixteenths one step was about six
10852               	; 	' SECONDS of his route, so nothing landed near the buzzer; in sixty-fourths
10853               	; 	' it is about one and a half. Keep hsp64 <= 128: hacc is under 64 on entry,
10854               	; 	' so 64 + 128 stays inside a byte and two drains always suffice.
10855               	; 	'
10856               	; 	' AND THE STEP IS CLAMPED TO THREE FRAMES' WORTH, WHICH IS NOT A DETAIL.
10857               	; 	' Two tests sample his position once a pass and neither interpolates:
10858               	; 	'
10859               	; 	'   ARRIVAL   `hdx < 6` around the escalator or the roof door -- an ELEVEN
10860               	; 	'             pixel window. A step over 10 px can jump clean across it and
10861               	; 	'             he never arrives at all.
10862               	; 	'   THE CATCH `hdd < CATCHR` is 12, a 23-wide band, and Kelly closes 4 of
10863               	; 	'             it himself -- so Harry over ~18 px could pass through the Kop
10864               	; 	'             between two passes without either sample being inside it.
10865               	; 	'
10866               	; 	' The clamp and the drains live in pace_step now, with the reasoning; the
10867               	; 	' numbers above are what sized them. Measured: TIME 02 on the lift screen
10868               	; 	' against TIME 04 on a light one when the clamp was 3, and 00 against 09
10869               	; 	' before any of this.
10870               	; 	'
10871               	; 	' The ESCALATOR RIDE is deliberately untouched: it returns above this,
10872               	; 	' clocked one step per pass to stay locked to the moving staircase. A rider
10873               	; 	' advanced by the frame delta either drifts off the treads or makes the
10874               	; 	' steps run backwards (CLAUDE.md 3A, DESIGN.md 0f). It is about 3% of his
10875               	; 	' journey.
10876               	; 	'
10877               	; 	' `hanim` still advances by hspd and is still an ODOMETER -- pixels
10878               	; 	' travelled, not time -- so the run cycle stays locked to the ground at any
10879               	; 	' rate. A 9 px step moves it exactly one pose of its 8 px beat.

11340               	;
11341               	; 	' ======================================================================
11342               	; 	' COLLISIONS -- pure arithmetic against RAM, no VDP reads
11343               	; 	' ======================================================================
11344               	; 	' Kelly's box is [kfh, kfh + kh) above the slab; an obstacle's is
11345               	; 	' [ohb, oht). The ball's inset hitbox is what makes 8..10 avoidable both
11346               	; 	' ways -- without it there is a height at which the ball can be neither
11347               	; 	' jumped nor ducked, and an unavoidable hazard is not difficulty.
11348               	; 	' ONE HIT PER CONTACT, WITH A REFRACTORY PERIOD.
11349               	; 	'
11350               	; 	' The overlap test is true on every frame the player is touching
11351               	; 	' something, so with no latch at all one clumsy cart charges nine seconds
11352               	; 	' several times over -- and what the player sees is the clock jumping by
11353               	; 	' 27, from which the only available conclusion is that the penalty is
11354               	; 	' broken.
11355               	; 	'
11356               	; 	' A latch that clears on the first non-overlapping frame is still not
11357               	; 	' enough, and the case that breaks it is the BOUNCING BALL: it rises off
11358               	; 	' the player between bounces, which is a genuine loss of contact, so a
11359               	; 	' player standing still under one is taxed on every single bounce while
11360               	; 	' being given no opportunity to do anything about it. Technically two
11361               	; 	' collisions; in play, one situation.

11734               	; 	' THE FLOOR CLEARS WHEN YOU ARE HIT, and stays clear until you re-enter
11735               	; 	' the screen. Nine seconds is a heavy penalty on a fifty-unit clock, and

11923               	; 	' AND THEY HAVE TO BE AT THE SAME HEIGHT, NOT MERELY ON THE SAME FLOOR.
11924               	; 	'
11925               	; 	' `hlv` does not change until a ride ENDS -- a crook stepping onto a
11926               	; 	' flight keeps the floor he left until he arrives at the next one. So
11927               	; 	' while he was most of a storey up or down the stairs he still counted as
11928               	; 	' standing on the floor he started from, and a Kop who ran over the head
11929               	; 	' of the flight arrested him through the floor. Reported from play:
11930               	; 	' "I run over top of him, even though we do not touch".
11931               	; 	'
11932               	; 	' It is the same shape of bug as the catch that fired at MAXIMUM
11933               	; 	' separation: a test that is right about one axis and silent about the
11934               	; 	' other, where the silent one happens to be true nearly all the time.

12051               	; 	' placed him at his old floor and then hid him again. That is not free.
12052               	; 	' CVBasic's SPRITE writes a RAM mirror which the vblank ISR copies to
12053               	; 	' VRAM, so a vblank landing BETWEEN the draw and the hide latches the
12054               	; 	' visible state for a frame -- and draw_actors is long (Kelly, Harry,
12055               	; 	' eight obstacles) while a pass on the lift screen spans two or three
12056               	; 	' frames, so it happened constantly. He flickered at the floor he had
12057               	; 	' just left, which reads as a drawing bug rather than as a journey.
12058               	; 	'

12060               	; 	' the mirror never holds a position to be caught with.

12271               	; 		' FOUR RUN FRAMES FROM TWO BITS of the animation counter, and no
12272               	; 		' divide -- `/` compiles to a real TMS9900 DIV (CLAUDE.md 3A) and
12273               	; 		' this is per-frame code. Two adjacent bits give 0,4,8,12.

13115               	; 	' Rows 21-23, 16 chars wide, centred: 48 characters whose PATTERNS are
13116               	; 	' poked directly, so a moving dot costs two writes and no name-table
13117               	; 	' traffic. With the flip (DESIGN.md 2a) this is how you know where Harry
13118               	; 	' is at all -- he can be one pixel off-screen and completely invisible.
13119               	; 	'
13120               	; 	' Rows 21-23 all sit in the THIRD screen third, so every scanner pattern
13121               	; 	' is at base 4096 and no third-selection arithmetic is needed.
13122               	; 	'
13123               	; 	' BOTH DOTS ARE WHITE and Kelly's BLINKS. The manual wants Kelly black
13124               	; 	' and Harry white, but this is the TMS9918's two-colours-per-8x1-cell
13125               	; 	' mode: a black dot and a white dot on the same pixel row of the same
13126               	; 	' character cannot both exist. Blinking distinguishes them with one
13127               	; 	' colour, which is what RallyX does with its player dot.
13128               	; 	' THE STEPS MOVE, AND EVERY ESCALATOR ON SCREEN MOVES WITH THEM. A flight
13129               	; 	' is twelve characters -- six per direction, sliced out of a rendered
13130               	; 	' 64x40 bitmap by genart.py -- so rewriting those twelve PATTERNS animates
13131               	; 	' the lot: 96 bytes, no name-table traffic, and the same cost whether one
13132               	; 	' flight is visible or ten. The phases slide the cells ALONG the slope, so
13133               	; 	' the steps travel up the flight rather than drifting sideways.

13159               	; 	' ONE PHASE PER PASS, AND NEVER MORE. There are four phases covering an
13160               	; 	' 8 px period, so advancing by the frame delta ALIASES: at fdv 2 the
13161               	; 	' pattern flips between two positions half a period apart and the
13162               	; 	' direction stops being readable, and at fdv 3 the sequence runs 0,3,2,1
13163               	; 	' -- the staircase visibly runs BACKWARDS, carrying its steps down while
13164               	; 	' the rider goes up. That is the wagon-wheel effect, and no amount of
13165               	; 	' phase arithmetic fixes it: a 4-phase cycle can only be stepped by 1.
13166               	; 	'
13167               	; 	' So the ANIMATION is the clock here, and the rider is paced from it --
13168               	; 	' see move_kelly, which advances him by the same fixed 2-and-1 per pass
13169               	; 	' rather than by fdv. Locking the two together is the only way they
13170               	; 	' cannot drift, and it is what "the player moves at the rate the steps
13171               	; 	' carry him" actually means. The cost is that a ride takes 36 passes
13172               	; 	' rather than 36 frames, so it slows down when the loop does -- which is
13173               	; 	' the honest behaviour for a machine that is carrying you.

13187               	; 	#if NES
13188               	; 	' A VBLANK OF ITS OWN, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE-SCREEN FLASH.
13189               	; 	'
13190               	; 	' PPUBUF is not flushed when it is written -- it ACCUMULATES for the whole
13191               	; 	' pass and the NMI empties it in one go, so every VPOKE the radar makes,
13192               	; 	' every HUD digit and this upload all land in the SAME vblank. And the
13193               	; 	' handler's copy loop does not stop when vblank ends: it runs to the end of
13194               	; 	' the descriptor and then writes PPUADDR and both PPUSCROLLs, which
13195               	; 	' mid-frame re-points the PPU's own render address. The rest of that frame
13196               	; 	' is drawn from the wrong place. On screen that is not a dropped tile, it
13197               	; 	' is the ENTIRE PICTURE jumping for a frame -- which is what has been
13198               	; 	' reported, repeatedly, as the screen flashing on an escalator.
13199               	; 	'
13200               	; 	' The arithmetic says it cannot be anything else. NTSC vblank is about
13201               	; 	' 2273 CPU cycles; NMI entry, the flicker test and OAM DMA spend ~560 of
13202               	; 	' them before a single byte is copied. A copy descriptor costs ~50 cycles
13203               	; 	' plus 14 a byte, so these six characters -- 96 bytes, because a tile is
13204               	; 	' SIXTEEN bytes in two bitplanes, not eight -- are ~1400 on their own.
13205               	; 	' That leaves about 270 cycles, or SIX single-byte pokes, for everything
13206               	; 	' else the pass queued. The radar alone beats that whenever a dot moves.
13207               	; 	'
13208               	; 	' Nothing smaller fixes it, because the overrun is per FRAME, not per
13209               	; 	' second: slowing the animation down just makes the bad frames rarer.
13210               	; 	' Splitting the six characters across two frames tears the staircase, and
13211               	; 	' only three of the six have a constant second bitplane, so dropping a
13212               	; 	' plane does not buy a frame's worth either. What DOES work is giving the
13213               	; 	' upload a vblank with nothing else in it: this WAIT flushes the pass's
13214               	; 	' radar and HUD writes, and the descriptor queued below is then almost all
13215               	; 	' the next vblank has to carry -- ~1960 cycles of 2273, inside the window
13216               	; 	' with room to spare.
13217               	; 	'
13218               	; 	' IT COSTS ONE FRAME A PASS, on the two screens that carry a flight and
13219               	; 	' nowhere else -- esc_tick has already returned on the other six. The
13220               	; 	' rider is paced from the animation rather than from the frame delta (see
13221               	; 	' below), so a slower pass slows the ride too and the two cannot drift.
13222               	; 	WAIT
13223               	; 	#endif

13225               	; 	' which cells move -- the step cells and the COMPOSITE copies of them
13226               	; 	' that cross a floor -- and groups them WEST then EAST, because only one
13227               	; 	' direction is ever on screen: screen 0 carries a west flight and screen
13228               	; 	' 7 an east one.
13229               	; 	'
13230               	; 	' THIS IS THE ONLY PER-PASS WORK UNIQUE TO THESE TWO SCREENS, and it is
13231               	; 	' `define_char`, which in bitmap mode is LDIRVM3 -- the TRIPLE copy, once
13232               	; 	' per screen third. It therefore costs three times what the character
13233               	; 	' count suggests, which is why these screens run slower than the rest.
13234               	; 	'
13235               	; 	' THE WEST SCREEN USED TO COST HALF AS MUCH AGAIN, because it carries TWO

13572               	;
13573               	; 	' ------------------------------------------------- the scanner's furniture
13574               	; 	' Without this the scanner is two dots in a void: you can see THAT Harry is
13575               	; 	' somewhere, but not what he is near, which is the one thing you actually
13576               	; 	' need when he is off-screen. Floor lines say which level, the slashes say
13577               	; 	' where that floor's escalator is, and the bar says where the elevator is --
13578               	; 	' exactly the three things the manual lists.
13579               	; 	'
13580               	; 	' FURNITURE AND DOTS ARE SEGREGATED BY PIXEL ROW ON PURPOSE, and a level
13581               	; 	' band is now FOUR rows, one per colour, because a pixel row carries
13582               	; 	' exactly one colour here:
13583               	; 	'
13584               	; 	'   +0  GREY    escalator head, and the elevator car
13585               	; 	'   +1  GREY    the air of that floor
13586               	; 	'   +2  GREY
13587               	; 	'   +3  YELLOW  the floor line -- and NOTHING else goes here
13588               	; 	'
13589               	; 	' THE FIRST THREE ROWS ARE THE FLOOR'S AIR AND EVERYTHING LIVES IN THEM:
13590               	; 	' the escalator's three-step diagonal, the lift car, and both actors, all
13591               	; 	' three pixels tall. They are grey in the table, and the Kop and the
13592               	; 	' crook recolour their own CHARACTER as they move (scan_mark) -- which is
13593               	; 	' what lets both of them fill the band instead of getting a pixel row
13594               	; 	' each. Eight pixels of this canvas is half a screen of the store, so
13595               	; 	' they are almost never in one character; when they are, they merge.
13596               	; 	'
13597               	; 	' Shrinking from six rows bought eight empty pixel rows, four above the
13598               	; 	' instrument and four below, so it no longer butts against the shop floor
13599               	; 	' above it or the bottom of the screen.
13600               	; 	'
13601               	; 	' The dots are erased by ANDing their bits out, so anything sharing a row
13602               	; 	' with one is rubbed away wherever an actor has passed -- which is why

13872               	; 	' A LEVEL BAND IS SIX PIXEL ROWS ON THE NES AND FOUR ON THE TI.
13873               	; 	'
13874               	; 	' It was six everywhere once. It shrank to four to buy eight empty pixel
13875               	; 	' rows -- four above the instrument and four below -- so the scanner did
13876               	; 	' not butt against the shop floor above it and the bottom of the screen.
13877               	; 	'

13879               	; 	' thirty rows to the TI's twenty-four, so the strip runs past the canvas to
13880               	; 	' the bottom edge and the grey either side of the instrument is real cells
13881               	; 	' rather than blank rows inside it. That gives the band its two rows back,

13883               	; 	' what "not quite so vertically thin" asks for.
13884               	; 	'

13886               	; 	' the last three rows, and there is nowhere to put the margin. So the band

14036               	;
14037               	; 	' Blank the canvas by WRITING zeros rather than copying 384 of them out
14038               	; 	' of ROM. This runs twice a game -- at setup and on a new Krook -- so a
14039               	; 	' loop costs nothing anybody can perceive, and it hands the fixed area
14040               	; 	' back the best part of half a kilobyte, which is the budget that
14041               	; 	' actually binds. Paced in bursts: a few hundred VDP writes in a single
14042               	; 	' frame are silently dropped (CLAUDE.md 3A).
14043               	; scan_wipe:
14044               cvb_SCAN_WIPE
14045               	; 	' THIS ADDRESS IS A CHARACTER CODE IN DISGUISE, AND IT WENT STALE.
14046               	; 	' 4096 is the pattern table's BOTTOM THIRD -- rows 16-23, which is
14047               	; 	' band 0 and the radar together -- and the canvas characters begin at
14048               	; 	' genart's SCAN_FIRST, so the base is 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8. It was
14049               	; 	' written out by hand as 4096 + 160*8 when SCAN_FIRST was 160; art
14050               	; 	' added later moved SCAN_FIRST to 208 and nothing moved this with it,
14051               	; 	' so the wipe zeroed the 48 characters BELOW the canvas and never
14052               	; 	' touched the canvas at all.
14053               	; 	'
14054               	; 	' Two of those forty-eight are STRUCTURE. ENDWALL is the building's
14055               	; 	' outside wall and SLABP is a pillar's cap. Blanking a pattern in ONE
14056               	; 	' THIRD leaves a character that draws correctly everywhere else and
14057               	; 	' falls back to its own background colour here -- so the GROUND FLOOR's
14058               	; 	' outside wall turned into plain green while the identical wall one
14059               	; 	' storey up was perfect, and the ground floor's pillars lost the brick
14060               	; 	' carried up through the bar above them. ENDWALL appears only on
14061               	; 	' screens 0 and 7, which is exactly why it was reported as happening
14062               	; 	' only on the escalator screens, mirrored side to side.
14063               	; 	'
14064               	; 	' The name table was correct the whole time. Probing it said so, four
14065               	; 	' times. It was the GLYPH that was empty, in one third only -- which a
14066               	; 	' probe that copies the character somewhere else to look at it cannot
14067               	; 	' see, because the copy renders from a different third's pattern.
14068               	; 	'
14069               	; 	' renumber.py rewrites this line from genart.SCAN_FIRST, and
14070               	; 	' checkstruct.py fails the build if the two disagree.
14071               	; 	#swa = 5760			' 4096 + SCAN_FIRST*8, the canvas patterns

14074               	; 	#if NES
14075               	; 	' AN NES TILE IS SIXTEEN BYTES, NOT EIGHT -- two bitplanes. DERIVED FROM
14076               	; 	' THE LINE ABOVE rather than written out again: renumber.py rewrites that
14077               	; 	' literal out of genart.SCAN_FIRST and checkstruct.py checks it, and a

14095               	; 	' by the same offset the PPU address uses, so it grows with the stride --
14096               	; 	' half of what it holds is the second bitplane, which this port never sets
14097               	; 	' and scan_or1 therefore never reads as ink.
14098               	; 	' AND THE CANVAS IS WIPED TO GREEN, NOT TO BLACK.
14099               	; 	'
14100               	; 	' On the TI a blank canvas is zeros and the COLOUR TABLE says what the
14101               	; 	' background is. There is no colour table here: a pixel's colour is its
14102               	; 	' two bitplane bits, so "green background" means plane 0 SET everywhere
14103               	; 	' and plane 1 clear -- index 1, which is the store's green in P0.
14104               	; 	'
14105               	; 	' THAT INVERTS THE SENSE OF EVERY FEATURE DRAWN ON TOP. The floor lines
14106               	; 	' add plane 1 to reach index 3 (gold), and the escalator diagonals CLEAR
14107               	; 	' plane 0 to reach index 0 (the backdrop, black) -- see scan_or1, which
14108               	; 	' is why it ANDs here and ORs on the TI. Writing zeros here instead would
14109               	; 	' leave the instrument black-on-black and the flights invisible.
14110               	; 	'

14112               	; 	' position within its tile decides which it is.
14113               	; 	' AND THE MARGINS ARE GREY, WHICH IS THE OTHER BITPLANE PAIR.
14114               	; 	'
14115               	; 	' The canvas is three character rows -- 24 pixel rows -- of which the
14116               	; 	' instrument uses the middle SIXTEEN (rows 4-19: four levels of four).

14123               	; 	' has to change: index 1 green is plane 0, index 2 grey is plane 1, and
14124               	; 	' the floor lines and flights work on top of those (scan_furn, scan_or1).
14125               	; 	'

14680               	;
14681               	; #if NES
14682               	; 	' ----------------------------------------------------------------------
14683               	; 	' THE ATTRIBUTE TABLE -- the NES's only way of giving two parts of the
14684               	; 	' screen different colours.
14685               	; 	'
14686               	; 	' 64 bytes at $23C0. Each byte covers FOUR character rows and four
14687               	; 	' columns, split into four 2x2 quadrants of two bits each: bits 0-1 top
14688               	; 	' left, 2-3 top right, 4-5 bottom left, 6-7 bottom right.
14689               	; 	'
14690               	; 	' The picture sits three rows down for overscan, which lands the regions
14691               	; 	' on block boundaries almost by luck:
14692               	; 	'
14693               	; 	'   byte row 0   name rows 0-3    the HUD is row 3  -> bottom quads P1
14694               	; 	'   byte row 1   name rows 4-7    the sky, top half -> P2, bottom -> P3
14695               	; 	'   byte rows 2+ name rows 8-29   the store         -> P0
14696               	; 	'
14697               	; 	' $50 is "bottom two quadrants on palette 1"; $FA is "top two on palette
14698               	; 	' 2, bottom two on palette 3", which is what splits the sunset into a
14699               	; 	' blue band over a warm one. Written as bare literals because this is the
14700               	; 	' one place the bit layout is visible, and naming them would hide it.
14701               	; 	'
14702               	; 	' 64 VPOKEs is 192 bytes of PPU queue, and WRTVRM waits when the 64-byte
14703               	; 	' buffer fills, so this paces itself across three frames and cannot
14704               	; 	' overrun vblank the way a single big SCREEN blit can.
14705               	; 	' A MESSAGE BOX GOES WHITE ON DARK BLUE, and the caller says which four
14706               	; 	' bytes in #nav.
14707               	; 	'
14708               	; 	' The text's paper is index 1 and its ink index 3 (see the font upload);
14709               	; 	' over the store those are P0's green and gold -- the same green the box is
14710               	; 	' sitting on, which is what made the messages hard to read. P1 is the HUD's
14711               	; 	' palette, dark blue and white, so pointing the box's attribute bytes at it
14712               	; 	' gives a message the same treatment as the score line.
14713               	; 	'
14714               	; 	' FOUR BYTES AND NOT ONE MORE. An attribute byte covers four characters by
14715               	; 	' four, and the box is sized and placed to cover exactly four of them
14716               	; 	' (gentitle.py BOX_ROW/BOX_COL/BOX_W): byte columns 2..5, which is name
14717               	; 	' columns 8..23. Anything wider would recolour shop floor beside the box.
14718               	; 	'
14719               	; 	' THIS IS A ROUTINE BECAUSE IT WAS WRITTEN OUT TWICE AND MISSED A THIRD
14720               	; 	' TIME. GOT HIM! kept the store's colours while the other boxes changed,
14721               	; 	' and nothing failed -- it is a readable message in the wrong palette.
14722               	; 	' checkmsg.py now fails the build if a message box is drawn without one of
14723               	; 	' these beside it.
14724               	; 	'
14725               	; 	' Nothing puts them back, because nothing needs to: every path out of a
14726               	; 	' message box redraws the screen, and draw_screen calls nes_attr, which
14727               	; 	' rewrites all sixty-four.
14728               	; nes_boxatt:
14729               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 3
14730               	; 		VPOKE #nav,85
14731               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14732               	; 	NEXT nai
14733               	; 	RETURN
14734               	;
14735               	; nes_attr:
14736               	; 	#nav = 9152			' $23C0
14737               	; 	' $55, NOT $50 -- ALL FOUR QUADRANTS ON P1, not just the bottom two.
14738               	; 	'
14739               	; 	' $50 put the HUD's own row (name row 2) on P1 and left rows 0-1 on P0.
14740               	; 	' That was invisible while text sat on the backdrop, and stopped being so
14741               	; 	' the moment the font gained a PAPER: rows 0-1 are blank cells, and a blank
14742               	; 	' cell is all paper, so they came out in P0's index 1 -- the store's GREEN
14743               	; 	' -- as a green band above the score line. Nothing is drawn up there, so
14744               	; 	' putting the whole byte on P1 costs nothing and the HUD reads as one band
14745               	; 	' of dark blue running into the sky.
14746               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 7
14747               	; 		VPOKE #nav,85
14748               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14749               	; 	NEXT nai
14750               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 7
14751               	; 		VPOKE #nav,170			' $AA -- the whole sky band on P2, no second palette
14752               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14753               	; 	NEXT nai
14754               	; 	FOR nai = 0 TO 47
14755               	; 		VPOKE #nav,0
14756               	; 		#nav = #nav + 1
14757               	; 	NEXT nai
14758               	; 	RETURN
14759               	; #endif

15225               	;
15226               	; 	' THE BONUS IS COUNTED OUT, NOT AWARDED. Dropping the whole sum into the
15227               	; 	' score in one frame tells the player a number; ticking the clock down a
15228               	; 	' unit at a time, with the score climbing and a beat under each step,
15229               	; 	' tells them what the number was FOR. It is the pay-off for every second
15230               	; 	' they saved, and every arcade game of this era spends a moment on it.
15231               	; 	'
15232               	; 	' It also costs nothing to get right: the loop already has to run down
15233               	; 	' `tsec`, so the animation IS the calculation, and the repeated-addition
15234               	; 	' note below stops applying -- each step adds one band's worth.
15235               	; 	'
15236               	; 	' x100 for Krooks 1-9, x200 for 10-15, x300 from 16. Two independent
15237               	; 	' sources agree on those bands; the manual's own wording suggests
15238               	; 	' 1-8 / 9-16 / 17+ and DESIGN.md 0 records the disagreement.
15239               	; 	'
15240               	; 	' IN UNITS OF TEN, WHICH IS WHAT THE SCORE IS COUNTED IN, so the bands are
15241               	; 	' 10 / 20 / 30 and not 100 / 200 / 300.
15242               	; 	'
15243               	; 	' They were 100 / 200 / 300 and paid TEN TIMES the right bonus -- 1,000 a
15244               	; 	' time unit where the original pays 100. `add_score` takes `#addv` in units
15245               	; 	' of ten (the prize beside it is `#addv = 5` for fifty points, and the bonus
15246               	; 	' Kop threshold is `#nextk = 1000` for ten thousand), so writing the band in
15247               	; 	' POINTS here shifted every tally one decimal place. Reported from play as
15248               	; 	' "it seems like you awarded 1000 per time unit left" -- exactly right.
15249               	; 	'
15250               	; 	' Nothing failed: 1,000 a unit is a plausible-looking number, the digits
15251               	; 	' all line up, and the only symptom is a score that runs away. The tell is
15252               	; 	' a constant written in a different unit from the routine it is passed to,
15253               	; 	' which is the same class of fault as the px-per-pass speeds in 3A.
15254               	; 	'
15255               	; 	' (This is also why the old comment here said "#bval MUST BE 16-BIT: 300
15256               	; 	' does not fit in a byte". At 10 / 20 / 30 it would, but it stays 16-bit
15257               	; 	' because `#addv` is, and a byte here would buy two bytes of ROM in
15258               	; 	' exchange for a truncation trap the next time somebody edits a band.)
15259               	; bonus_count:

15378               	; 	' Two were tried. The bench's own ending for this variant rose a fourth,
15379               	; 	' to 2,542 Hz, and a square wave there is a shriek -- the same fault the
15380               	; 	' pickup was rewritten for. Dropping it an OCTAVE BELOW the ticks, to
15381               	; 	' 518 Hz, was reported the same way, and that one cannot be too high by
15382               	; 	' any measure: it is the lowest note in the effect.
15383               	; 	'
15384               	; 	' So the complaint is not the pitch, it is the extra note. A tally is
15385               	; 	' arithmetic, and arithmetic finishes when the last term is added; a
15386               	; 	' flourish after it is a second event the player has to interpret, and
15387               	; 	' the HUD has already said the clock is empty. The count stops when the
15388               	; 	' counting stops.
15389               	;
15390               	; 	' `calc_bonus` USED TO LIVE HERE and computed the whole sum by repeated
15391               	; 	' addition, to dodge two hazards at once: `tsec * bmul` is an 8-bit
15392               	; 	' product (a 50-unit capture in the x300 band pays 15,000, six times past
15393               	; 	' a byte), and multiplying properly lands on the MPY/r0 hazard where a
15394               	; 	' 16-bit variable read straight after being multiplied returns the
15395               	; 	' product's high word. Counting the bonus out a unit at a time (above)
15396               	; 	' removes the multiply entirely rather than working around it -- the loop
15397               	; 	' the player watches IS the arithmetic.
15398               	; 	'
15399               	; 	' It also fixed the last-tick case for free: `bn_loop` tests `tsec = 0`
15400               	; 	' on entry, where the old `FOR bi = 1 TO tsec` would have run its body
15401               	; 	' once and paid a full multiplier for no time at all (CLAUDE.md 3A).

15597               	;
15598               	; 	' Silence every channel FIRST. SOUND latches, and the per-channel decay
15599               	; 	' counters are not ticked inside this loop -- a tone still sounding when
15600               	; 	' the pause starts would hang for its whole duration, which is the classic
15601               	; 	' CVBasic sticky-audio failure.

15603               	; 	' ticked by the main loop, so anything still sounding when the loop stops
15604               	; 	' -- for a capture, a death, the bonus count -- sustains for as long as
15605               	; 	' whatever replaced the loop takes. That is where the long beep over the
15606               	; 	' bonus tally came from: not the tally's own note, which turns itself off
15607               	; 	' after every unit, but a footstep or a hit that was still ringing when

15614               	; 	' NOISE channel. So a step ringing when Harry was caught was never turned

15728               	;
15729               	; 	' A SOUND STILL PLAYING WHEN THE ROUND ENDS IS ALLOWED TO FINISH.
15730               	; 	'
15731               	; 	' This used to open with a bare `GOSUB snd_off`, which cut it dead. That
15732               	; 	' was not an accident: the decay counters are ticked by the MAIN LOOP, and
15733               	; 	' this pause REPLACES the main loop, so a tone left latched with nothing
15734               	; 	' ticking it hangs for the full ninety frames -- the sticky-audio failure
15735               	; 	' this game has already shipped twice. The answer is to DRAIN the counters
15736               	; 	' rather than to stop silencing.
15737               	; 	'
15738               	; 	' CLEAR THE PENDING LATCHES FIRST. sf* flags are sounds that have not
15739               	; 	' happened yet; left set, the drain below would START one and the pause
15740               	; 	' would end with a fresh note ringing into the next round.
15741               	; 	'
15742               	; 	' THEN TICK sfx_tick WHOLE, not some decay-only part of it. The five
15743               	; 	' counters do not all live in one place: sot, sht and spt are a block at
15744               	; 	' the tail, but spz (the prize arpeggio) and swt (the jump warble) tick up
15745               	; 	' among the code that starts sounds. Draining only the tail would finish a
15746               	; 	' footstep and still cut the arpeggio, which is the one effect with a
15747               	; 	' phrase worth saving. Calling the whole routine also leaves the write
15748               	; 	' order on CHANNEL 2 alone, which spz and spt share.
15749               	; 	'
15750               	; 	' EVERY THIRD FRAME, because the main loop runs about 2.5 frames per pass
15751               	; 	' and this loop waits one frame per turn. Ticking every frame would play
15752               	; 	' everything at two and a half times its tuned speed. Three frames a tick
15753               	; 	' is ~17% slow and gives 30 ticks against the longest effect's 20 passes.
15754               	; 	'
15755               	; 	' THE LOOP COUNTS TICKS, NOT FRAMES, which is what makes the pacing free.
15756               	; 	' Counting 91 frames and firing on every third needs a second counter, an
15757               	; 	' increment and a test -- 48 bytes, on a fixed area with 66 left. Counting
15758               	; 	' 31 TICKS of three WAITs each is the same 93 frames and the same three
15759               	; 	' frames per tick, with none of that. The duration changes by two frames.
15760               	; 	'
15761               	; 	' snd_off still runs at the END, as the backstop for anything the drain
15762               	; 	' did not finish.
15763               	; pause_beat:
15764               cvb_PAUSE_BEAT
15765               	; 	GOSUB snd_pend
15766 F998 06A0  32 	bl @jsr
     F99A A980     
15767 F99C F970     	data cvb_SND_PEND

     F9A2 2155

16056               	; 	' the jump sweep: divisor falling = pitch rising
16057               	; 	' THE JUMP IS A WARBLE, NOT A SWEEP -- testsounds variant A, measured off

16127               	; 	' THE LOW-TIME WARNING IS SILENT. There was a beep a second under ten, and
16128               	; 	' it was the wrong instrument for the job: the last ten seconds are the
16129               	; 	' busiest part of a round, so a repeating tone arrives exactly when the
16130               	; 	' player most needs to hear the hazards, and it fought the prize arpeggio
16131               	; 	' for channel 2 as well. The flash says the same thing and says it in the
16132               	; 	' place the player is already looking.
16133               	;
16134               	; 	' FOOTSTEPS ARE NOISE, AND ON THE NOISE CHANNEL -- testsounds variant A.
16135               	; 	'
16136               	; 	' They were two alternating TONES on channel 0, which is neither what the
16137               	; 	' original does nor a good use of a channel: the recording says a footstep
16138               	; 	' is a short burst of white noise, and channel 3 was sitting unused while
16139               	; 	' the footsteps and the jump sweep shared channel 0 and had to take turns.
16140               	; 	'
16141               	; 	' TESTSOUNDS RUN D: a SHORT tick at the measured RATE.
16142               	; 	'
16143               	; 	' The two dials are independent and both were tried at the bench. The
16144               	; 	' 2600 plays a 64 ms burst every 165 ms -- six a second -- and variant A
16145               	; 	' copies both. Ten a second was tried on the way here and reads as
16146               	; 	' hurrying rather than running. What D changes is not the cadence but the
16147               	; 	' TICK: two frames rather than four, and a notch louder to carry at half
16148               	; 	' the length. Same six a second, less of it.
16149               	; 	'
16150               	; 	' EIGHT A SECOND, AND THE ACCUMULATOR NOW CARRIES ITS REMAINDER.
16151               	; 	'
16152               	; 	' sfw counted pixels and the trigger did `sfw = 0`, THROWING AWAY whatever
16153               	; 	' was past the threshold. kspd is about four pixels a pass, so a threshold
16154               	; 	' of 17 did not fire at 17 -- it fired at the first multiple past it, about
16155               	; 	' 20, and every rate this was ever set to came out slower than the number
16156               	; 	' said: the "six a second" was 5.2 and the "ten" that read as hurrying was
16157               	; 	' really 8.7. Subtracting the threshold instead keeps the fraction, so the
16158               	; 	' rate is what it claims to be at any walking speed.
16159               	; 	'
16160               	; 	' MEASURED OFF THE COLECOVISION: 14 px, about 7.4 a second.
16161               	; 	'
16162               	; 	' It was 15 px and 6.9 a second, picked between an 8.0 that read as
16163               	; 	' slightly hurried and a 6.1 that read as trudging -- a judgement between
16164               	; 	' two other judgements, with nothing underneath it. The ColecoVision
16165               	; 	' recording settles it: footfalls land every 0.130 s across a twelve-second
16166               	; 	' continuous run, which is 7.7 a second, and that is the one finding in the
16167               	; 	' whole sound analysis the method resolves EXACTLY -- a rhythm rather than a
16168               	; 	' pitch, counted off the RMS track rather than inferred from a spectrum.
16169               	; 	' (colecosounds variant 1A; assets/sfx/sfxref-coleco.md has the working.)
16170               	; 	'
16171               	; 	' 104 px/s over 14 px is 7.43 a second. 13 px would give 8.00, and 7.7 sits
16172               	; 	' almost exactly between them -- so this is the nearer of the two, and it is
16173               	; 	' also the one that does not walk back into the 8.0 that was rejected by ear.
16174               	; 	'
16175               	; 	' WHY THE GAME KEEPS A DISTANCE AND THE BENCH KEEPS A CADENCE. The bench
16176               	; 	' plays a fixed eight frames between steps because it has no walking to tie
16177               	; 	' them to; the game accumulates PIXELS TRAVELLED, so the feet keep time with
16178               	; 	' the legs when he is slowed or stopped. Matching "7.4 a second" therefore
16179               	; 	' means matching it AT HIS WALKING SPEED, and assumes the ColecoVision's
16180               	; 	' crook walks at ours -- which the recording cannot confirm.
16181               	; 	'
16182               	; 	' The dial is this one constant and the subtraction below, which must stay
16183               	; 	' threshold + 1 or the carry is wrong.
16184               	; 	'
16185               	; 	' SOT = 2 IS THE SHORTEST TICK THERE IS, and 1 is SILENCE. The decay block
16186               	; 	' below runs LATER IN THE SAME sfx_tick, so a count of 1 is decremented to
16187               	; 	' zero on the pass that set it and the note-off fires before the sound has
16188               	; 	' lasted any time at all. 2 survives to the next pass, which is one pass of
16189               	; 	' sound -- about 42 ms against the bench's 33, as close as a per-pass timer
16190               	; 	' gets, and the reason the bench and the game cannot sound identical.
16191               	; 	'
16192               	; 	' Register 4 is white noise at the fastest rate.
16193               	; 	'
16194               	; 	' VOLUME 9, WHICH IS UNDER EVERYTHING ELSE ON PURPOSE. The hit, the prize
16195               	; 	' and the jump are 12 and 13, and they happen ONCE; footsteps play for the
16196               	; 	' whole round. At 13 they were level with the events they are supposed to
16197               	; 	' sit beneath, so the effects that carry information had nothing to stand
16198               	; 	' out from. The tone version was 7 for the same reason -- noise does read
16199               	; 	' quieter than a tone at the same number, which is why this is 9 and not

16399               	;
16400               	; 	' EVERYTHING BELOW THIS LINE IS ASSEMBLED INTO BANK 1, so the INCLUDE order
16401               	; 	' is load-bearing and nothing but data may follow it.
16402               	; 	'
16403               	; 	' THE FONT IS NOW IN THE BANK TOO, and it used to be deliberately outside:
16404               	; 	' keeping one readable thing in bank 0 means a bank-selection mistake shows
16405               	; 	' as "text survives, art does not" rather than a uniformly blank screen,
16406               	; 	' which is a genuinely useful thing to have when a bank goes wrong.
16407               	; 	'
16408               	; 	' THE FONT HAS A BANK OF ITS OWN, and the reason is not its size.
16409               	; 	'
16410               	; 	' Bank 1 was FULL -- six spare bytes of 8,192 -- which shut the door on
16411               	; 	' moving anything else out of the fixed area, and the fixed area is the
16412               	; 	' only budget that cannot be grown (linkticart writes exactly three
16413               	; 	' loader pages and discards the rest; they are the 32K expansion's RAM at
16414               	; 	' >A000, not cart ROM). A second bank costs a bigger cart -- five pages
16415               	; 	' round up to eight, so 32 KB becomes 64 KB -- and buys back the ability
16416               	; 	' to keep evacuating data out of code.
16417               	; 	'
16418               	; 	' THE FONT IS THE RIGHT TENANT because it is read ONCE. Two DEFINEs copy
16419               	; 	' it into VRAM at setup and nothing looks at it again, so it is the only
16420               	; 	' block here that can sit on a page which is not permanently mapped. See
16421               	; 	' setup_font: bank 2 is selected for those two statements and bank 1 for
16422               	; 	' the whole of the rest of the program.
16423               	; 	'
16424               	; 	' EVERYTHING ELSE STAYS IN BANK 1, because everything else is read during
16425               	; 	' play -- art on a screen crossing, templates on a band blit, the lookup
16426               	; 	' tables every pass. One permanently-mapped bank for all of it means
16427               	; 	' there is no switch to miss.
16428               	; 	#if TI994A
16429               	; 	BANK 2
16430      01EC     BANK_0_FREE:	EQU >fffe-$

16569               	; 	' THE COLOUR TABLE, 472 bytes of the same value ($14 = black ink on dark blue).
16570               	; 	'
16571               	; 	' Loaded with DEFINE COLOR 32,59,font_col, which is ONE synchronous call that
16572               	; 	' writes all three screen thirds (define_color always does the LDIRVM3 triple
16573               	; 	' copy). It replaced a VPOKE loop that wrote this one value 1,416 times paced by
16574               	; 	' 24 WAITs -- the largest scripted delay in the boot, and the reason the title
16575               	; 	' screen used to fill in visibly rather than appearing at once.
16576               	; 	'

16578               	; 	' whatever follows in ROM as colour data, with no error at build or run time.

16904               	; 	' AND THE TITLE'S DISPLAY LIST, for the same reason as the font: walked
16905               	; 	' once by title_draw, at boot and on a return to the title, and never
16906               	; 	' during play. title_draw selects bank 2 around its walk.
16907               	; 	'
16908               	; 	' ITS MESSAGE BOXES DID NOT COME WITH IT. They are the same format and
16909               	; 	' were in the same generated file, which is what made this worth doing
16910               	; 	' carefully: they are walked when a ROUND ENDS, mid-game, so on bank 2
16911               	; 	' they would have returned bytes from the wrong page at the moment a life
16912               	; 	' is lost -- and with no error at build or run time. gentitle.py now
16913               	; 	' writes them to title.bas below, which stays in bank 1.
16914               	; 	INCLUDE "titledl.bas"
16915               	; 	' ==================================================
16916               	; 	' THE TITLE SCREEN, AS A DISPLAY LIST
16917               	; 	' Generated by assets/gentitle.py -- do not edit here.
16918               	; 	'
16919               	; 	' row, col, length, then `length` bytes; 255 ends.
16920               	; 	' Walked by title_draw only.
16921               	; 	'
16922               	; 	' LIVES IN BANK 2, with the fonts, because it is read ONCE
16923               	; 	' -- at boot and on a return to the title. title_draw
16924               	; 	' selects bank 2 around its walk and restores bank 1.
16925               	; 	' The message boxes in title.bas are the same format and
16926               	; 	' CANNOT come with it: they are read when a round ends.
16927               	; 	' ==================================================
16928               	;
16929               	; title_tbl:
16930               cvb_TITLE_TBL
